name: Device client hints (DPR, Viewport, Memory)
plain: Opt-in headers carrying DPR, viewport width, device memory and color scheme.
meaning: Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width, Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-Device-Memory and Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme let servers pick image sizes and themes before first paint, and also hand the same fingerprint bits to every server that asks.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can learn your screen density, window width, memory and light or dark mode in Chromium browsers
limits.user_action: Nothing. The browser sends it only after the site asks for it
can: Ask your browser to send screen sharpness, window width and device memory with each request
See if you prefer dark mode
Pick the right image size and theme before the page shows
cannot: Get any of it unless the site asks first and the browser agrees
Work in Firefox or Safari, which do not send these
Learn exact memory, since it is rounded
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send these. Firefox and Safari, including all iPhone browsers, do not.

story.what_it_is: Browsers can send screen density, window size and memory with each page request when a site asks.

marketing.name: Client Hints
marketing.pitch: Servers can opt in to receive details about the device, so they can send the best version of a page first time.

story.for_you: You never see it. If a site asks, your browser tells the server how sharp your screen is and how wide your window is. The server can then send the right sized picture right away.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to ship the right image size and a lighter page for weaker devices, with no extra round trip. It also tells them things about your device that add to a fingerprint, which is why a site must ask first.

use_cases.example: A store gets the screen sharpness and window width, then sends one right sized product photo, so a phone does not download a huge desktop image.
A browser game portal reads device memory and sends a lighter build to low memory phones, so the game does not crash on load.
A news site picks a dark or light page from the color scheme hint and avoids a bright flash on first paint.
A video site picks a starting quality from window width and screen sharpness before the player even loads.
An ad server picks an ad size matching the window width, and may combine other hints to recognize a device again.
A tool records memory and screen hints to show what kind of devices visitors use, and to plan support.
A developer tests a site on a low memory phone to see that the lighter version really arrives.
